# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 65 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 65 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_065_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 65 describes the corrective function of the Angel of Punishment. This is a theodicy: suffering in life is not random cruelty but targeted discipline from a loving God. The mechanism is corrective (not punitive-final): the purpose of torment is purification (*katharisthē apo tēs anomias*).

The list of afflictions in 65:2 — losses of money, goods, illnesses, adversities — reflects the Roman Christian experience of economic vulnerability, persecution, and social instability. Hermas reads these hardships as divinely pedagogical.

The crucial distinction in 65:4-5: those who have "God in their hearts" respond to affliction by repenting — and thus live; those with "nothing in themselves" have no capacity to respond and remain tormented. This is not arbitrary — their suffering is proportionate and purposive, but without the internal resource of faith, they cannot benefit from it.

EMET and LOGOS handle "lives to God for the remainder of their days" similarly. SOPHIA retains this as it adds the temporal specificity of "remainder of their days" for *tas loipas hēmeras*.

---

## Similitude 6, Part 3 — The Angel of Punishment

**65:1** "Now, the angel of punishment — to whom those who fall away from God are delivered — torments every such person in proportion to his deeds. Such is his method of punishment: the great sinner receives many torments, and the one whose sins are few receives few torments."

**65:2** "How then does the angel of punishment torment the soul of the sinner?" "He afflicts him," he said, "through all the sufferings that this person is worthy to undergo in his life — various losses and losses of money and goods, and various illnesses and many afflictions, and every kind of adversity. For from all such things arise sufferings and diseases and various troubles."

**65:3** "These things come about," he said, "not from any malice toward the person, but because the Lord wishes to save him. Since the Lord loves him, he hastens to chastise him, so that this person may be purified of the great iniquity that is in him."

**65:4** "Now those who are servants of God and have God in their hearts — when they perceive that they are afflicted in any matter, they reflect on their iniquities and evil deeds, and repent. And having repented, they live to God for the remainder of their days."

**65:5** "But the man who has nothing in himself and has no resistance against the angel of punishment — he remains in his torments to the end of his days."

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus rendering of EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA, with rulings recorded in the Disagreement Log.*
